lead: A field effect transistor (FET) controls current by an electric field, not by feeding current into a control terminal. In an n-channel FET, a negative or positive gate voltage changes the width of a conducting channel between source and drain. A wider channel carries more drain current; a narrower channel carries less. The gate draws almost no current, so input resistance is very high, often around 10¹⁰ Ω. FETs appear in sensors, radio front ends, power supplies and digital circuits. The two common families are the junction FET (JFET) and the metal-oxide-semiconductor FET (MOSFET).
prereq: You need: 4.1 for the reverse-biased junction and depletion region, and 4.3 for the BJT comparison.

blocks.text: An n-channel JFET is a bar of n-type silicon called the channel. Two p-type regions are diffused into its sides and joined as the gate. One end of the channel is the source, the other end is the drain. The gate and channel form a p–n junction. In normal operation the gate is negative with respect to the source, so this junction is reverse biased. The reverse bias creates a depletion region around the gate. This region has few free electrons and acts as an insulator. As V<sub>GS</sub> becomes more negative, the depletion region grows and the channel narrows. A narrow channel has higher resistance, so drain current I<sub>D</sub> falls. At one negative gate voltage the depletion regions meet and close the channel. That voltage is V<sub>GS(off)</sub>, also called the pinch-off voltage V<sub>P</sub>. For an n-channel JFET, V<sub>GS(off)</sub> is negative, often −2 V to −8 V. The saturation current at V<sub>GS</sub> = 0 is I<sub>DSS</sub>. The gate current is only reverse leakage, so gate input resistance is very high. The device is unipolar: channel current uses one carrier type, electrons here.
With V<sub>DS</sub> high enough, I<sub>D</sub> depends mainly on V<sub>GS</sub>. The transfer characteristic is a square law:

blocks.where: I<sub>D</sub> is drain current in mA; I<sub>DSS</sub> is the saturation current at V<sub>GS</sub> = 0 in mA; V<sub>GS</sub> is gate-source voltage in V; V<sub>GS(off)</sub> is the pinch-off voltage in V, negative for an n-channel JFET.

blocks.text: At V<sub>GS</sub> = 0, I<sub>D</sub> = I<sub>DSS</sub>. At V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>GS(off)</sub>, I<sub>D</sub> = 0. The figure plots this curve for I<sub>DSS</sub> = 8 mA and V<sub>GS(off)</sub> = −4 V. The drain characteristics plot I<sub>D</sub> against V<sub>DS</sub> for fixed V<sub>GS</sub>. At small V<sub>DS</sub>, the channel acts as a voltage-controlled resistor; this is the ohmic region. As V<sub>DS</sub> rises, the drain end of the channel pinches first, and I<sub>D</sub> almost stops rising. This is the saturation region, where the square law is used. The gate-channel junction must stay reverse biased, so V<sub>GS</sub> should not go positive by more than about 0.5 V; otherwise gate current flows. The symbol for an n-channel JFET has a vertical channel line, source and drain leads, and a gate arrow pointing inward. The arrow shows the p-to-n direction of the gate junction. Some syllabi call the JFET a voltage-controlled resistor in the ohmic region.

An n-channel enhancement MOSFET has two n+ regions, source and drain, in a p-type substrate. A thin silicon dioxide layer covers the area between them, and a metal or poly-silicon gate sits on top. The oxide is an insulator, so gate and channel form a capacitor. At V<sub>GS</sub> = 0, no conducting path exists between source and drain; the device is off. When V<sub>GS</sub> is positive, it attracts electrons to the substrate surface under the oxide. Above a threshold voltage V<sub>T</sub>, enough electrons form an n-type inversion layer. This layer joins source and drain and conducts. A larger V<sub>GS</sub> makes the inversion layer richer and raises I<sub>D</sub>. In saturation:

blocks.where: I<sub>D</sub> is drain current in A or mA; k is a device constant in A/V²; V<sub>GS</sub> is gate-source voltage in V; V<sub>T</sub> is threshold voltage in V.

blocks.text: For an n-channel enhancement MOSFET, V<sub>T</sub> is positive, often 1 V to 3 V. A depletion MOSFET has a built-in channel, so it conducts at V<sub>GS</sub> = 0 and can be turned off by a negative V<sub>GS</sub>. The gate oxide gives input resistance of order 10¹⁰ Ω or higher. The device is also called an IGFET or MOS device. Its symbol uses a broken channel line for enhancement mode, with a gap between gate and channel; the substrate arrow points inward for n-channel.

A BJT is current-controlled: base current controls collector current. Its base-emitter junction is forward biased, so the base draws current. A FET is voltage-controlled: gate-source voltage controls drain current, and the gate draws almost no current. A BJT uses electrons and holes, so it is bipolar. A FET uses mainly one carrier type, so it is unipolar. FETs give higher input resistance and lower input current. BJTs give higher transconductance for the same bias current and are often cheaper for simple analog circuits. The choice depends on the circuit: a BJT suits a simple audio amplifier, while a MOSFET suits a high-impedance sensor input or a digital gate. In exam answers, do not say a MOSFET has gate current; the oxide blocks it. Do not say a JFET gate junction is forward biased in normal operation.

figure.caption: Transfer characteristic of an n-channel JFET with I_DSS = 8 mA and V_GS(off) = −4 V. The current is zero at −4 V and rises as a square law to 8 mA at 0 V.

spec.aria: Plot of the JFET transfer characteristic for IDSS = 8 mA and VGS(off) = −4 V: drain current is zero at −4 V and rises as a square law to 8 mA at 0 V.

examples.question: An n-channel JFET has I<sub>DSS</sub> = 8 mA and V<sub>GS(off)</sub> = −4 V. It is biased at V<sub>GS</sub> = −2 V with R<sub>D</sub> = 2.2 kΩ and V<sub>DD</sub> = 15 V. Find I<sub>D</sub>, V<sub>DS</sub> and the transconductance g<sub>m</sub>. Use the saturation region.
steps: Check bias: V<sub>GS</sub> = −2 V lies between V<sub>GS(off)</sub> = −4 V and 0 V, so the JFET is on and the square law applies.
I<sub>D</sub> = I<sub>DSS</sub>(1 − V<sub>GS</sub>/V<sub>GS(off)</sub>)² = 8 mA × (1 − (−2 V)/(−4 V))² = 8 mA × (1 − 0.5)² = 8 mA × 0.25 = 2 mA.
Drain resistor drop V<sub>RD</sub> = I<sub>D</sub>R<sub>D</sub> = 2 mA × 2.2 kΩ = 4.4 V.
V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>RD</sub> = 15 V − 4.4 V = 10.6 V. This is greater than V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>GS(off)</sub> = −2 V − (−4 V) = 2 V, so saturation is confirmed.

g<sub>m</sub> is the change in I<sub>D</sub> for a small change in V<sub>GS</sub>. First g<sub>m0</sub> = 2I<sub>DSS</sub>/|V<sub>GS(off)</sub>| = 2 × 8 mA / 4 V = 4 mS. Then g<sub>m</sub> = g<sub>m0</sub>(1 − V<sub>GS</sub>/V<sub>GS(off)</sub>) = 4 mS × (1 − 0.5) = 2 mS.
examples.answer: The JFET has I<sub>D</sub> = 2 mA, V<sub>DS</sub> = 10.6 V and g<sub>m</sub> = 2 mS.
examples.check:
IDSS = 8.0
VGSoff = -4.0
VGS = -2.0
RD = 2.2
VDD = 15.0
ID = IDSS * (1 - VGS / VGSoff) ** 2
VDS = VDD - ID * RD
gm0 = 2 * IDSS / abs(VGSoff)
gm = gm0 * (1 - VGS / VGSoff)
print(ID)
print(VDS)
print(gm)

traps: V<sub>GS(off)</sub> is negative for an n-channel JFET. Writing +4 V instead of −4 V flips the square-law result.
The JFET square law holds in saturation, not in the ohmic region at very small V<sub>DS</sub>.
I<sub>DSS</sub> is the saturation current at V<sub>GS</sub> = 0, not the current at any V<sub>DS</sub>.
Do not expect gate current in a MOSFET; the oxide insulates the gate. Gate current appears only through leakage or oxide damage.
V<sub>T</sub> and V<sub>GS(off)</sub> are not the same: V<sub>T</sub> is the enhancement-MOSFET threshold, while V<sub>GS(off)</sub> is the JFET pinch-off voltage.

quiz.a: I<sub>DSS</sub> is the drain current at V<sub>GS</sub> = 0 with V<sub>DS</sub> large enough to keep the JFET in saturation. It is the maximum drain current for that device.

quiz.q: Why is the gate-channel junction of an n-channel JFET kept reverse biased?
quiz.a: The gate is p-type and the channel is n-type. A negative V<sub>GS</sub> reverse biases the junction, so gate current is only leakage. The reverse bias also widens the depletion region and controls channel width.

quiz.q: State the difference between the ohmic and saturation regions in the JFET drain characteristics.
quiz.a: In the ohmic region, small V<sub>DS</sub> makes the channel act like a voltage-controlled resistor, so I<sub>D</sub> rises with V<sub>DS</sub>. In saturation, the drain end pinches and I<sub>D</sub> is almost set by V<sub>GS</sub> alone.

quiz.q: An n-channel JFET has I<sub>DSS</sub> = 10 mA and V<sub>GS(off)</sub> = −5 V. Find I<sub>D</sub> at V<sub>GS</sub> = −2 V in saturation.
An n-channel enhancement MOSFET has V<sub>T</sub> = 2 V and k = 0.5 mA/V². Find I<sub>D</sub> in saturation at V<sub>GS</sub> = 4 V.
quiz.a: I<sub>D</sub> = k(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>)² = 0.5 mA/V² × (4 V − 2 V)² = 0.5 × 4 mA = 2 mA.

quiz.q: Explain why a FET has much higher input resistance than a BJT.
quiz.a: In a JFET the gate junction is reverse biased, and in a MOSFET the gate oxide is an insulator. Both leave only tiny leakage current. A BJT has a forward-biased base-emitter junction, so its base draws a normal current.

quiz.q: What happens if V<sub>GS</sub> of an n-channel JFET is made more negative than V<sub>GS(off)</sub>? Does the square law still apply?
quiz.a: The depletion regions overlap completely and the channel is closed, so I<sub>D</sub> is about zero. The square law is a model for V<sub>GS</sub> between V<sub>GS(off)</sub> and 0 V; outside that range it no longer applies.

beyond: Not for the exam. CMOS uses complementary n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs; it is the base of most digital chips, from microcontrollers to memory. Power MOSFETs switch currents in chargers and motor drives, and wide-bandgap devices such as GaN HEMTs are used in fast chargers. Search next for CMOS inverter, MOSFET capacitances, body diode, and JFET used as a low-noise sensor input. The same field-effect idea appears in ISFET pH sensors and in memristor research.
